title: A safe, scalable cure for established HIV infection

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an intervention for people already living with HIV that safely produces durable control of the infection without continuous treatment and can be delivered affordably at scale. It includes two distinct possible outcomes: treatment-free remission, in which replication-competent virus may remain but stays controlled, and eradication, in which no replication-competent virus remains. Demonstrating remission would not by itself establish eradication.

Conceptual basis from the supplied research: HIV can persist as integrated genetic material in long-lived cells, including reservoirs that are difficult to locate or reach. A cure would therefore need to eliminate the virus capable of restarting infection or establish lasting control over it. These biological premises explain the intended innovation, but the retained source contains no scientific text with which to verify them.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: a safe, accessible intervention that reliably produces durable treatment-free remission would remove the need for continuous HIV medication during that remission. Its revolutionary value would depend on combining durable control with acceptable safety and broad delivery; a rare outcome following an intensive procedure would not establish that capability. The supplied research describes existing HIV management as ordinarily requiring lifelong treatment, although the retained evidence does not independently substantiate that clinical background.

Conditional downstream possibility: reduced onward transmission could provide an additional benefit, but it would require evidence about infectiousness after the intervention, the durability of control and how widely the intervention could be delivered. Freedom from continuous medication does not alone establish freedom from transmission risk. Likewise, treatment-free remission should not be interpreted as proof that every infectious viral reservoir has been eliminated.

missing_breakthrough.text: Scientific challenge, synthesized from the supplied research: the missing capability is reliable elimination or permanent control of replication-competent HIV across the reservoirs that can sustain established infection. The concrete barriers include locating persistent infected cells, reaching relevant reservoirs, and ensuring that virus left behind cannot restart productive infection. An intervention must achieve this while preserving an acceptable safety profile.

Engineering and clinical challenge, synthesized from the supplied research and review: any successful mechanism must become a reproducible intervention suitable for a broad population, with manageable delivery requirements and affordable access. The research frames cancer-directed stem-cell transplantation as an exceptional, hazardous route to remission rather than a scalable treatment for HIV alone. That transplant indication and risk context could not be verified from the retained document and should remain qualified.

Measurement challenge: showing that no virus was detected in sampled material is weaker than showing that no replication-competent virus remains anywhere in the person. Reservoir assessment, observation for viral rebound and long-term clinical follow-up address different questions. Together they can strengthen a remission claim and constrain uncertainty about eradication, but negative sampling alone cannot prove complete viral elimination. This distinction is a scientific assessment retained from the review, rather than a finding verified in the accessible source.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a report attributed to Gaebler et al., “Sustained HIV-1 remission after heterozygous CCR5Δ32 stem cell transplantation,” listed as published in Nature on 1 December 2025, with DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09893-0. The research attributes more than six years of remission in one person to this report. These bibliographic details and the quantitative outcome are supplied assertions: the retained document does not provide the paper or abstract needed to verify them.

The review found that the retained copy of the cited PubMed page contains only a cookie interstitial. Consequently, the earlier statement that an abstract was accessed must be corrected: no usable abstract is retained. The paper's identity, remission duration, transplant indication and safety context could not be established from that document content. This access limitation does not show that the reported result is false.

Evidence interpretation: if independently verified, the reported single-person remission would support the biological possibility of prolonged treatment-free control in that clinical setting. It would not establish safe, affordable treatment for a broad population, nor would remission alone prove eradication. The supplied search record contains no freshness evidence, so it cannot establish whether a safe, scalable cure is available as of 11 November 2026 or whether later developments change the picture.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: controlled studies should show years of treatment-free viral suppression after an acceptably safe intervention in a broad range of people with established HIV infection. A study protocol would need to define the required duration, eligible populations, acceptable failure rate and safety thresholds in advance. These are proposed criteria for convincing evidence, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Safe intervention enables years of treatment-free suppression across broad populations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification: combine intensive reservoir sampling with repeated monitoring for viral rebound and extended follow-up for late adverse effects. Report sustained remission separately from evidence bearing on eradication, and specify assay limits and sampling coverage. Independent replication should test whether outcomes persist across investigators, clinical settings and participant groups. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated outcomes distinguish remission from eradication within stated verification limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: successful trials should also demonstrate a feasible delivery pathway, reproducible intervention quality and an explicit affordability benchmark. A result confined to people receiving intensive treatment for a serious blood cancer would not satisfy the intended broadly deliverable HIV cure. The acceptable cost, infrastructure requirements and balance of benefit against harm remain to be defined.
completion_criteria.label: Broadly feasible delivery demonstrates reproducible quality and benchmarked affordability

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: INF-01, “A broadly protective HIV vaccine,” addresses prevention of HIV infection, whereas INF-02 addresses infection already established. They share a pathogen and could contribute to complementary control strategies, but protection against acquisition would not demonstrate clearance or durable control of an existing infection.

Roster-based comparison: INF-11, “A safe, broadly effective treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B,” shares the goal of durable control of persistent viral infection without ongoing treatment. The conceptual overlap concerns persistence and the evidence needed to distinguish treatment-free control from elimination. HIV and hepatitis B remain distinct infections with distinct cure endpoints. Only INF-11's title was supplied, so its mechanisms and detailed completion criteria cannot be inferred here.

Roster-based comparison: INF-07, “Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections,” emphasizes treatment breadth across viruses; INF-02 emphasizes durable resolution of established HIV infection. Antiviral activity alone would not establish treatment-free remission. INF-12, “Very short, reliable curative treatment for active and latent tuberculosis,” similarly seeks a finite route to cure, but concerns a different pathogen and disease biology. These entries remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: The cited paper's identity, publication details and reported more-than-six-year remission require verification against usable scientific content.
The transplant indication, treatment risks and broader history of exceptional transplant-associated HIV remissions remain unverified in the retained evidence.
No usable source text independently supports the supplied biological background on integration, long-lived reservoirs or their accessibility.
The empty freshness record leaves present-day availability and subsequent developments unresolved.
Study duration, population coverage, acceptable rebound rates, safety thresholds, affordability benchmarks and delivery requirements remain to be defined.
The supplied material does not establish how infectiousness would change after the proposed intervention.

brief.title: A safe, widely available cure for HIV
possible: People living with HIV could keep the infection controlled for years without continuous HIV medication, through a safe intervention affordable enough for widespread use.
This could mean remission, where HIV remains under lasting control, or eradication, where all virus capable of restarting infection has been eliminated.
why: HIV treatment ordinarily continues for life. Lasting control after treatment ends would free people from continuous medication. Affordable delivery would extend that benefit across a broad population.

sources.showed: A single-person report describes prolonged HIV remission after a transplant of stem cells, which produce blood and immune cells.
sources.cited_for: The report supports the possibility of prolonged HIV control after transplantation.
sources.not_established: Reliable control through a safe, affordable intervention for broad use still requires demonstration.

sources.who: Ming Jie Lee and RIO Trial collaborators
sources.showed: This preprint reports sustained control without HIV medication in a quarter of participants receiving long-acting antibodies, proteins that block HIV infection.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports antibody treatment as a route toward sustained control after HIV medication stops.
sources.not_established: Reliable, lasting control across broad populations and elimination of infectious HIV remain to be demonstrated.

sources.who: The authors studying long-term HIV post-intervention control
sources.showed: A small group maintained HIV control for years after antibody treatment and stopping HIV medication. Infectious virus persisted, and one participant later lost control.
sources.quote: Altogether, these results indicate that all PICs had reservoirs of inducible infectious proviruses that were not decreasing, and that theoretically could contribute to viral rebound in vivo.
sources.cited_for: Long-lasting control can coexist with persistent infectious virus.
sources.not_established: Reproducing this outcome reliably in a broad population remains an open challenge.

sources.showed: HIV remained undetectable for 32 months after HIV medication stopped following a donor stem cell transplant for cancer. Treatment for transplant complications continued.
sources.quote: To date, plasma viral load has remained undetectable for 32 months after the interruption of antiretroviral treatment.
sources.cited_for: This case demonstrates prolonged remission after a cancer-directed transplant.
sources.not_established: Safe delivery for people receiving treatment for HIV alone and complete viral elimination still require demonstration.

shown: Researchers studying exceptional responses to antibody treatment describe HIV control lasting beyond 7.5 years without continuous HIV medication. These participants began HIV treatment relatively early. Infectious virus remained in their bodies.
missing: A safe intervention must reliably prevent HIV from restarting infection across the places where infected cells persist.
Independent studies must reproduce lasting control across a broad range of people.
A delivery pathway must combine consistent treatment quality with affordable access.

milestones.label: Safe, years-long control across broad populations
milestones.explanation: Controlled studies would have to demonstrate years of control without continuous HIV medication across diverse populations, with acceptable safety. This would establish reliable benefit beyond exceptional cases.

milestones.label: Replicated outcomes establish remission and assess viral elimination
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to combine extensive sampling, monitoring for returning virus and long-term safety follow-up, stating test limits. This would establish reproducibility and clarify evidence for remission or eradication.

milestones.label: Broad delivery achieves consistent quality and defined affordability
milestones.explanation: Successful trials would also have to demonstrate feasible delivery, reproducible treatment quality and a stated affordability benchmark. This would establish whether the intervention can reach a broad population.

uncertain: The duration, acceptable rate of returning virus, safety thresholds and affordability benchmarks needed to judge success remain undefined.
Negative samples leave uncertainty about infectious virus elsewhere in the body.
How treatment-free control would affect the risk of transmitting HIV remains unresolved.

page.title: HIV remission without antiretroviral therapy
page.definition: An intervention controls established HIV infection without continuing antiretroviral therapy (ART), meeting published population efficacy, safety and delivery targets. Remission permits HIV capable of restarting infection to remain; eradication requires removal of that virus.

goal.need: In 2025, 78% of people living with HIV were accessing treatment. ART ordinarily continues for life because infected cells can retain virus capable of restarting infection. An intervention that sustains control after ART withdrawal would remove the requirement for continuing ART during remission.

figures.note: Intervals are the uncertainty ranges reported by UNAIDS.

completion.title: An HIV-remission product meets IAS optimum efficacy, safety and delivery-setting targets.
completion.criterion: Meet the IAS optimum clinical-efficacy, safety and delivery-setting targets: HIV RNA <50 copies/mL without ongoing ART in ≥90% of treated participants, average relapse <2% per year and remission >3 years; no grade 3 or 4 adverse events, significant irreversible adverse events <1%, and delivery in primary or secondary settings capable of providing ART. Grade 3 and 4 events are severe and life-threatening events, respectively.
completion.set_by: International AIDS Society multi-stakeholder consultation, published in Table 2 of its HIV cure combination-therapy target product profile; these targets appear in a table.
completion.basis: The optimum profile supplies population efficacy, toxicity and delivery benchmarks beyond exceptional individual remission. These are development targets, not a regulatory definition of cure or proof of eradication. The numerical profile was written for combination therapy; separate cell and gene therapy profiles exist.

milestones.title: An intervention prevents detectable SHIV rebound for 196 days after ART withdrawal in macaques.
milestones.criterion: Prevent confirmed detectable plasma virus through day 196 after ART withdrawal in SHIV-infected rhesus macaques; the assay detection limit was 2.3 log10 RNA copies/mL. SHIV combines simian and human immunodeficiency-virus components. In the 2018 study, ART began 7 days after infection and stopped at week 130, 16 weeks after the final antibody dose. PGT121 plus vesatolimod produced no rebound in 5/11 macaques, compared with 0/11 sham controls.
milestones.set_by: Borducchi and colleagues, published preclinical study endpoint in Figure 4a; this protocol tested an antibody and an immune stimulant in SHIV-infected macaques.
milestones.threshold_quote: Numbers and percentages of animals that show viral rebound by day 196, defined as any confirmed detectable viral load, are depicted.

milestones.title: An HIV-cure candidate is administered to people in an authorised clinical study.
milestones.criterion: A candidate enters an authorised clinical study and is administered to people with established HIV. FDA recognises phase 1 as the human safety-and-dosage stage. A 2021 study infused CCR5-edited CD4 T cells into 14 participants; no serious adverse events were reported. EBT-101, an in-vivo HIV gene-editing intervention, was administered to 6 participants in a phase 1/2 study; its July 2024 conference report described rebound in 3 participants undergoing ART interruption at 3.5, 4 and 16 weeks. The EBT-101 results were not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, clinical research stages and Investigational New Drug process; the regulatory framework described here is US-specific.

milestones.title: A person remains off ART for ≥24 weeks with HIV RNA ≤400 copies/mL at ≥two-thirds of measurements.
milestones.criterion: Remain off ART for ≥24 weeks, with plasma HIV RNA ≤400 copies/mL at ≥two-thirds of measurements; higher values must be followed by suppression through week 24. CHAMP identified 67 such controllers among >700 participants in 14 studies; this classification alone does not establish an intervention effect. Transplantation reports describe one man with >6 years of remission after transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia and another person with 32 months of undetectable HIV RNA, while receiving ruxolitinib for chronic graft-versus-host disease.
milestones.set_by: CHAMP investigators, published posttreatment-controller definition, subsequently used in cell-therapy research.
milestones.threshold_quote: remained off ART for ≥24 weeks posttreatment interruption and maintained viral loads ≤400 copies/mL for at least two-thirds of the time points.

milestones.title: An intervention delays HIV rebound versus placebo through a 20-week ART interruption at two-sided α=0.05.
milestones.criterion: Show superiority over placebo for time to protocol-defined rebound through 20 weeks after ART interruption, using two-sided α=0.05. RIO defined rebound by two consecutive HIV RNA measurements >100,000 copies/mL, six consecutive weeks >1,000 copies/mL, or other protocol-defined events. In 68 men randomised 34:34 to 3BNC117-LS plus 10-1074-LS or placebo, estimated proportions without rebound at week 20 were 75% versus 11% (hazard ratio 0.09; 95% CI 0.04–0.21; P<0.001). A peer-reviewed secondary-outcomes paper corroborates the preprint result.
milestones.set_by: RIO investigators, amended protocol and statistical analysis plan for NCT04319367; this endpoint was specified for broadly neutralising antibodies.
milestones.threshold_quote: All statistical results were two-tailed, with a 5% significance level.

milestones.title: An intervention keeps HIV RNA <200 copies/mL off ART for >2 years in ≥20% of recipients.
milestones.criterion: Maintain HIV RNA <200 copies/mL without ART in ≥20% of recipients, with average relapse <10% per year and remission >2 years. This is the IAS minimum clinical-efficacy target, not the complete minimum product profile. Three selected antibody recipients maintained control for >6.5 years, >7.5 years and 2.5 years; infectious virus persisted in all three. These selected cases do not establish population response or relapse rates.
milestones.set_by: International AIDS Society multi-stakeholder consultation, Table 2, minimum clinical-efficacy row; published for combination therapy and stated only in a table.

not_found: No fixed affordability price or delivery-volume threshold was found in the accessible IAS target product profile or NIH cure goals.
The full 2025 cell-based and gene-based therapy target product profile could not be opened, so its numerical thresholds could not be checked.
No single published completion test covering efficacy, safety, affordability and delivery across all three approaches was identified.

results.finding: One stem-cell transplant recipient maintained undetectable HIV RNA off ART for more than 6 years.
results.detail: The transplant was given for acute myeloid leukaemia. Plasma viral load was monitored regularly after ART interruption.
results.quote: So far, HIV remission has been sustained for more than 6 years with undetectable plasma HIV RNA.

results.finding: One stem-cell transplant recipient maintained undetectable HIV RNA off ART for more than 6 years.
results.detail: This single selected case does not establish a response rate among recipients or an average annual relapse rate.
results.quote: So far, HIV remission has been sustained for more than 6 years with undetectable plasma HIV RNA.

results.finding: Three people with HIV received broadly neutralizing antibodies in clinical trials.
results.detail: The participants were identified from previously reported clinical trials and subsequently underwent ART interruption.
results.quote:
Three PICs were identified following administration of bNAbs and 
subsequent analytical treatment interruption (ATI) as part of previ-
ously reported clinical trials4,5,10.

results.finding: One antibody recipient remained off ART with undetectable HIV RNA for 130 weeks.
results.detail: ID142 had two minor blips and later restarted ART after rebound. The selected case does not establish an intervention effect.

results.finding: Three selected antibody recipients maintained ART-free control for at least 2.5 years.
results.detail: The three participants were selected post-intervention controllers, so they do not establish the proportion of all recipients responding or the average annual relapse rate.
results.quote:
Here, we describe three exceptional post-intervention 
controllers (PICs) who maintained ART-free virological control for >6.5 years 
(ongoing), >7.5 years (ongoing) and 2.5 years following administration of 
broadly neutralizing antibodies.

results.finding: One stem cell transplant recipient had undetectable HIV viremia 32 months after ART interruption.
results.detail: Plasma testing was at least monthly. The participant reported two brief episodes of pre-exposure prophylaxis during follow-up and received ruxolitinib for graft-versus-host disease.

results.finding: One stem cell transplant recipient had undetectable plasma viral load 32 months after ART interruption.
results.detail: This single selected case does not establish the proportion of recipients achieving remission or an average annual relapse rate. The participant reported two brief episodes of pre-exposure prophylaxis.
results.quote: To date, plasma viral load has remained undetectable for 32 months after the interruption of antiretroviral treatment.

results.finding: PGT121 plus vesatolimod prevented rebound through day 196 in 5 of 11 SHIV-infected rhesus macaques.
results.detail: All 11 sham controls rebounded. ART began on day 7 after infection and stopped at week 130, 16 weeks after the final antibody dose; the plasma assay detection limit was 2.3 log10 RNA copies/mL.
results.quote: In the combination PGT121+GS-9620 group, however, only 6 of 11 (55%) animals rebounded by day 196 following ART discontinuation.

results.finding: Eight SHIV-infected infant macaques had no evidence of replicating virus 1 year after treatment interruption.
results.detail: The antibody, CCR5-blockade and ART combination began 72 hours after infection. ART stopped at week 27 after antibody washout; the plasma assay detection limit was 26 RNA copies/mL.
results.quote: Following the treatment of infants with viraemia at 72 h post-infection with the combination of broadly neutralizing antibodies, ART and leronlimab, no subsequent evidence of replicating or latent virus and antiviral immunity was observed 1 year after treatment interruption.

results.finding: CCR5-edited CD4 T cells were infused into 14 participants with chronic HIV infection in a phase I study.
results.detail: The registered study used participants’ own cells edited outside the body. No serious adverse events related to infusion were reported.
results.quote: According to the protocol, all participants received a single infusion of 10 billion cells, except participant 204, who received only 6.6 billion cells because of insufficient ex vivo T cell expansion during manufacturing.

results.finding: EBT-101 was administered to 6 participants with HIV in a phase 1/2 study.
results.detail: The conference presentation reported treatment-emergent adverse events and post-dose findings. It was not peer reviewed.
results.quote:
• Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE) related to drug
• There were 9 TEAEs in 6 participants

results.finding: In 68 participants, 3BNC117-LS plus 10-1074-LS delayed rebound versus placebo through week 20 (hazard ratio 0.09).
results.detail: Participants interrupted ART after infusion; 34 were assigned to each arm. The reported p value was <0.0001.
results.quote: Participants in arm A were 91% less likely to rebound than were those in arm B (hazard ratio 0·09; 95% CI 0·04-0·21, p<0·0001).
